claims.claim: The internet is a large network of interconnected computer networks that communicate using shared protocols; it is the technical infrastructure, not the same thing as the web.
The web is a service built on top of the internet; email and other services also run on the same infrastructure.
An Internet Service Provider (ISP) is a company that operates interconnected routers and connects a customer's network to other ISPs' networks, giving reach to the rest of the internet.
Every device on the internet has a unique numeric identifier called an IP address (Internet Protocol address); IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four dot-separated numbers such as 192.0.2.172.
IPv6 increases the address size from 32 bits to 128 bits to support a far greater number of addressable nodes, addressing IPv4 address exhaustion.

The Internet Protocol delivers blocks of data called datagrams (packets) from a source to a destination across interconnected networks, using addressing and fragmentation/reassembly, and provides no reliability, flow control, or sequencing itself.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a reliable, connection-oriented, ordered host-to-host protocol that runs on packet-switched networks and recovers from lost, damaged, or duplicated data using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and flow control.
A router is a device that forwards packets between networks by reading the destination address and passing each packet toward its target.

Ideally there is one protocol at the internet level (IP), which stays independent of the underlying hardware so diverse networks can interconnect; higher-level functions are best implemented at the endpoints (end-to-end principle).

ARPANET, the forerunner of the internet, sent its first computer-to-computer signal between UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute on October 29, 1969, and used packet switching so messages did not depend on any single node.
TCP/IP, designed by Vint Cerf and Robert Kahn in the 1970s, became the standard, and by January 1983 enough networks had interconnected using it that ARPANET had evolved into the internet.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact year and place TCP/IP was 'developed' (1974 Cerf-Kahn paper vs DARPA's '1975 at Stanford').
positions: The 1974 Cerf-Kahn paper is the usual date cited for the TCP design.
DARPA's ARPANET feature says Cerf and Kahn had developed TCP/IP by 1975 at Stanford.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids over-precision: it says TCP/IP was designed by Cerf and Kahn in the 1970s and that ARPANET switched fully to TCP/IP by January 1, 1983 (flag day), both of which the sources support.

sourceRecords.title: How does the Internet work?
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the network-of-networks description, ISPs as interconnected routers, IP address as unique device identifier (four dot-separated numbers, e.g. 192.0.2.172), routers forwarding packets like a post office, and the key internet-vs-web distinction ('The Internet is an infrastructure, whereas the Web is a service built on top of the infrastructure'). Facts synthesized; no MDN wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 791: Internet Protocol (DARPA Internet Program Protocol Specification)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports IP's scope: deliver a package of bits (an internet datagram) from source to destination over interconnected networks; implements addressing and fragmentation/reassembly; 32-bit fixed-length addresses; explicitly provides no end-to-end reliability, flow control, or sequencing.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 793: Transmission Control Protocol (DARPA Internet Program Protocol Specification)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports TCP as a highly reliable host-to-host protocol on packet-switched networks that adds ordered, reliable delivery, flow control, and recovery from lost/damaged/duplicated data on top of IP's unreliable datagram service.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
sourceRecords.notes: Supports IPv6 as successor to IPv4, increasing address size from 32 bits to 128 bits to support many more addressable nodes and more addressing hierarchy; motivates IPv4 address exhaustion.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 1958: Architectural Principles of the Internet
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the principle that there should ideally be one protocol at the internet level (IP), kept independent of hardware medium and addressing so diverse networks interconnect, and the end-to-end argument that higher-level functions belong at the endpoints.

sourceRecords.title: ARPANET
sourceRecords.provider: DARPA (U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency)
sourceRecords.notes: Public-domain U.S. government source. Supports history: first computer-to-computer signal between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute on Oct. 29, 1969; four initial nodes; packet switching adopted so messages did not depend on any single node; Cerf and Kahn developed TCP/IP; by January 1983 ARPANET had evolved into the internet; ARPANET decommissioned 1990.
